explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Paul, Silvanus and Timothy command the church to keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life, one "not in keeping with the tradition you received from us" (2 Thessalonians 3:6). It's a command given in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ. Nothing in the verse is about questions or travel. It's about how a person is living.

Good guess if you've ever dodged a tough meeting, but that's not in the verse. The command is about a brother who leads an undisciplined life that isn't in keeping with the tradition they received (2 Thessalonians 3:6). Paul never says anything about asking elders questions here. I bet a lot of bakers would have stamped that one too, and I'd be first in line.

Nope, no suitcases in this verse. The command is to keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life (2 Thessalonians 3:6). Travel never comes up. Paul's team is talking about how a brother lives, not where he goes.
Close, but this one flips it. Paul says the opposite: his team did not "eat anyone's food without paying for it" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). They paid their own way. That's the example they're setting.

False is right, baker. Paul says they did not eat anyone's food without paying for it (2 Thessalonians 3:8). No freebies, no tabs left behind. They covered their own meals while they were with the church.

Burden, yes. Paul says they worked "night and day so that we would not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). That's the whole reason for the long hours. They didn't want to weigh on the church.
Not quite. Nobody in this verse is worried about being a stranger. They worked night and day so they "would not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). Burden is the word Paul picks.

Rival sounds dramatic, I'll give you that. But there's no rivalry in this verse. Paul's team worked night and day "so that we would not be a burden to any of you" (2 Thessalonians 3:8). The word is burden.

explanations.answer: To be an example to imitate
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says they had the right to support, "but we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9). They had the right and chose to work anyway. The text gives that reason, and no other.

explanations.answer: To prove they were the strongest
explanations.explanation: Ha! No muscle contest here. Paul gives the reason himself: "we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9). Nobody in this passage is flexing. They wanted to show the church how to live.

explanations.answer: To save up for the next trip
explanations.explanation: A fair thought, since people do save up for things. But Paul never mentions a trip here. He says they worked "to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate" (2 Thessalonians 3:9). That's the reason the text gives.

explanations.answer: Anyone unwilling to work shall not eat
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says the command was given even while they were there: "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). Notice it's about being unwilling. That's a different thing from being unable. It's a short command, and it's easy to remember.

explanations.answer: Anyone who works shall rest each week
explanations.explanation: Rest is a good thing, but that's not what Paul quotes here. The command he gave them was, "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). It's about those who won't work. Weekly rest isn't in this verse.

explanations.answer: Anyone who eats shall share with others
explanations.explanation: Sharing is lovely, friend, but Paul isn't quoting that one. The command was, "If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10). It's about work, and what happens when someone is unwilling to do any.

True, friend. Paul writes that he hears some of them are "leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies" (2 Thessalonians 3:11). Accomplishing nothing is right there in the verse. He's heard it as news from the church.

Careful, this one's in the verse. Paul says, "For we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives, accomplishing nothing, but being busybodies" (2 Thessalonians 3:11). So he does say they're accomplishing nothing. It's only some of them, not the whole church.

Quietly, yes! Paul commands and urges them "to begin working quietly to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). Remember the busybodies from the verse before. Quiet work is the other direction from that. And it comes by the Lord Jesus Christ.

I get it, "harder" sounds like what a boss says. But Paul's word is different: "to begin working quietly to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). The call is to begin working quietly, not to work harder.

Teamwork is nice, but that's not the word in this verse. Paul says to "begin working quietly to earn their own living" (2 Thessalonians 3:12). Earning their own living is the point. Quietly is the word that goes in the blank.

explanations.answer: Don't get tired of doing good
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul writes, "But as for you, brothers, do not grow weary in well-doing" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). The message turns here, from the ones accomplishing nothing to the ones doing right. Keep going, friend.
Slow and steady is a fine habit, but Paul says something else. He writes, "do not grow weary in well-doing" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). The word is weary. It's about not giving out while doing good.
Bragging is a bad habit, I'll give you that. But it isn't what this verse says. Paul writes, "do not grow weary in well-doing" (2 Thessalonians 3:13). He's encouraging them to keep at it.
Yes, baker. Paul says, "do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). The distance is real, but so is the family tie. He's still a brother.

This is the one Paul rules out. He says, "do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). Keeping distance in verse 14 doesn't turn a brother into an enemy. He's still a brother.
Not quite, friend. Nothing in the verse puts him up front. Paul says, "do not regard him as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother" (2 Thessalonians 3:15). He's a brother who needs to be admonished.
Not this time. Paul doesn't limit it. He writes, "may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way" (2 Thessalonians 3:16). That's every time, not only the hard ones.
False is right, friend. Paul writes, "may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way" (2 Thessalonians 3:16). There's no limit to hard times. At all times means all times.

True, baker. Paul writes, "This greeting is in my own hand" and "This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write" (2 Thessalonians 3:17). It's how the church could recognize a letter from him. Right there in the verse.

Look again, this one's in the verse. Paul says, "This greeting is in my own hand" and then, "This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write" (2 Thessalonians 3:17). So he does call it his mark in every letter. The true answer was waiting right there.
